Purpose
DeepseekSparseSWAMetadataBuilder.build()
creates one empty
FlashMLASchedMeta
per DeepSeek-V4 layer type. The first
flash_mla_with_kvcache
call of each type runs FlashMLA's tile-scheduler planner, and the later layers of that type reuse the plan (the comment calls it "shared across all ~60 layers of that type within a decode step").
However, the builder runs once per KV cache group. With the packed KV cache layout, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's sliding-window caches are spread over 8 groups, and each group builds its own holders. So the planner runs once per (group, layer type). A torch-profiler trace of one TP8 decode step shows 18 planner launches in the target model (before layers 0-9 and 20-27) and 3 in the DSpark drafter (one per draft layer), where 4 are enough.
get_mla_metadata_kernel
is a single 32-thread block with a serial loop over the SM partitions, and every launch sits in front of its layer's attention. On H20 it takes 16.6 µs per launch at 1 request and about 41 µs at 64 requests.
A plan depends on the batch shape and on the values of the decode
topk_length
/
extra_topk_length
. FlashMLA's interface allows reuse only while those values stay the same, but it asserts only shapes and config. Across the KV cache groups of one metadata build pass the values do match:
The SWA lengths come from the same query and sequence lengths, window, valid-token mask and
replay_start
. Each group builds the mask from its own slot mapping, but every sliding-window group writes each scheduled token, so the masks agree;
replay_start
is one tensor passed to every builder.
The top-k lengths count the valid entries each index layer writes. Every decode top-k path fills the entries past a row end derived from
seq_lens
and
next_n
alone with -1 (for example
rowEnd
in
csrc/libtorch_stable/sampler.cu
), under the same valid-token mask. So each index layer of a compress ratio yields
min(rowEnd, topk)
.
That second point is also why a group's same-type layers can already share one plan today, though they take their top-k from different index layers.
This PR lets the groups share the holders:
MRV2's
build_attn_metadata
passes one dict to every group's
CommonAttentionMetadata
, next to the existing
_token_to_req_indices_cache
.
The sliding-window builder takes its plan holders from that dict, keyed by its block size, causality and index width.
What stays as before:
Callers that do not pass the dict (the V1 runner, the draft metadata refresh of the autoregressive speculator) keep one plan per group.
DBO micro-batches and the DSpark drafter build in separate passes, so they never share a plan.
SM100 does not take this path: it defaults to FlashMLA mega attention, which does not use these plan holders.
Planner launches per decode step drop from 21 to 4.
Duplicate check.

for
tile_sched
,
FlashMLASchedMeta
,
get_mla_metadata
,
tile scheduler
and
planner flashmla
shows no PR that shares the plan across KV cache groups.
Related:
#58762
(RFC
#58638
) reuses Mamba/GDN metadata across KV cache groups in the same
build_attn_metadata
loop. This PR does the same for DeepSeek-V4's FlashMLA plans, which are built per group however many groups there are.

Status: draft.
Opened early to get direction feedback before investing in
the long-term version. The optimization itself works and is measured; the
path-selection policy is deliberately provisional and will be reworked (see
Roadmap
). Comments on the approach are more useful than comments
on the gating details, which are expected to change.
Overview
On SM90 the DSv4.1 candidate-consuming indexers have no paged sparse scoring
kernel, so they score the entire compressed context per decode row and then
mask down to the candidate blocks. This adds an opt-in path that gathers the
candidate K from the paged FP8 indexer cache and scores only the candidates.
Implements the alternative-A direction of
#61830
.
Not a duplicate:
#57858
and
#57859
implement candidate-only scoring for ROCm
(gfx950); this is the SM90/CUDA counterpart called for in
#61830
.
Claims
Claiming only what is measured at this stage:
At ~1M context, 9 concurrent requests on 8x H20 (TP8): the four
candidate-consuming indexer layers drop from
9.57 ms to 3.05 ms
per step,
and per-step time from
39.04 ms to 31.53 ms
(profiler-derived).
Selected top-k sets are equivalent to the existing dense score-then-mask
path.
Default behaviour is unchanged: the feature is off by default, and
unsupported shapes or platforms fall back to dense rather than failing.
Known cost: a single-request step is about
11.6% slower
than dense, since
the candidate path carries a per-step fixed cost. The provisional workload
gates exist to avoid that region until a better policy lands.
Validation
Setup: 8x H20, TP8, DSv4.1,
num_speculative_tokens=5
, ~1M token context.
With
1 + 5 = 6
tokens per request the SM90 paged kernel takes the flatten
path, so one active request contributes roughly 6 decode rows.
Kernel / unit
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_candidate_gather_cudagraph.py
pytest tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py
test_candidate_gather_cudagraph.py
(new): gather + scoring + remap under
CUDA graph capture and replay.
test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py
(extended): dense vs. candidate-only
equivalence of the selected top-k set.
Equivalence
With
VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_FORCE=1
, the selected top-k index set matches
the dense path on identical inputs. Note that
#61830
's alternative-A hoped for
bit-identical results; this verifies set equivalence instead, since the
gather-then-score path uses a different scoring kernel and top-k tie-breaking
can differ (documented in the module docstring).
Server-level
Real
vllm serve
at ~1M context, torch profiler traces collected with the
feature off and on:
Configuration
Per step
Four consumer indexer layers
Dense (feature off)
39.04 ms
9.57 ms
Candidate-only (feature on)
31.53 ms
3.05 ms
at 9 concurrent requests (~54 decode rows).
To reproduce, enable on an SM90 FP8-cache deployment:
export
VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_DECODE=1
export
VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_ROWS=16
Validation still in progress
— explicit about what the numbers above do
not
yet cover, and queued in this order:
A profiler-free end-to-end throughput/latency A/B (current timings are
profiler-derived).
Model-level accuracy evaluation plus an independent numerical reference
(correctness evidence so far is top-k set equivalence against vLLM's own
dense path).
Cross-hardware validation on SM90 parts other than H20 — the reason no
crossover constant is hardcoded.
I will keep appending results to this PR as they come in.
Details
Why the dense path is wasteful here.
The candidate-consuming indexers are
handed a small, fixed-width candidate set, but SM90 lacks a paged sparse
scoring kernel, so they score the whole context and discard everything outside
the candidate blocks. The discarded work grows linearly with context length
(~98% of the scoring work at 1M context, per
#61830
).
What the new path does.
Gather each candidate block's K from the paged FP8 indexer cache into a
compact per-row buffer.
Score only the gathered candidates with the existing non-paged FP8 scoring
kernel.
Remap the selected columns back to request-local token positions, so the
output is identical in meaning to the dense path.
Scope kept narrow on purpose.
Only the candidate-consuming indexers take
the new path; the candidate-source and pre-candidate indexers stay dense, as
they have no candidate set to exploit. Restricted to SM90 with an FP8 indexer
cache and no context parallelism — SM100 already has native sparse kernels,
and all other platforms keep today's behaviour.
Tradeoff, and why the current gating is provisional.
Dense cost scales
with
rows x context
, while candidate scoring is dominated by a per-step
fixed cost, so the crossover tracks scanned work relative to the candidate
width rather than context length alone. Since the profitable threshold is
hardware-dependent, this PR does not bake in a device-specific constant and
instead exposes host-side gates (details collapsed below), treating them as a
stopgap, not the intended final interface
. Defaults impose only
shape-level lower bounds, and the H20 values above are reported as
measurements, not recommended defaults.
Known structural limitation.
Path selection is host-side per step and is
not
graph-aware: a fully-captured CUDA graph fixes whichever path was active
at capture time.
FORCE
exists to make that behaviour testable. This is the
main reason the feature ships disabled by default.
Workload gates (provisional)

Meaning

Roadmap
This PR is a reviewable first increment, not the finished design:
Graph-aware path selection
, so the choice is not frozen by full CUDA
graph capture. This is the blocker for enabling the feature by default.
Replace the manual env gates
with an automatic, device-independent
decision (calibration or a cost model), with proper small-batch protection
instead of a hand-set row threshold.
Longer term
, a native paged sparse scoring kernel for SM90 is the
cleaner fix than gather-then-score — a much larger change. This PR first
establishes whether the candidate-only direction is worth it, which the
numbers above suggest it is.
Happy to run specific concurrency levels, context lengths, or accuracy
benchmarks on request.

Overview
Add a Triton candidate-only decode scoring path for DeepSeek V4.1 on SM90,
reading FP8 K directly from the paged indexer cache instead of scoring the
full context and masking it afterwards.
Related to
#61830
. This is a separate implementation from the gather-based
prototype in draft
#62000
: it avoids the intermediate candidate-K buffer.
The flag is off by default (
VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE=1
to enable).
Claims
On H20 TP8 with ~1M input tokens, the evalscope A/B below measured a
9.6–23.8% reduction in mean ITL
across concurrency 1/2/4/8.
Consumer logits use 16,384 candidate columns instead of the full compressed
context. The candidate-source layers, pre-candidate layers and prefill path
are unchanged.
Path selection uses configuration checks, not capture-time context lengths.
Live lengths and page tables remain device inputs during CUDA graph replay.
These results cover the measured long-context workload, not a general
no-regression claim. Accuracy and shorter-workload checks are still pending.
Validation
Environment
Machine: 8x NVIDIA H20 96GB, TP8; driver 535.161.08, CUDA 13.0
Software: torch 2.14.0+cu130, triton 3.8.0, deep_gemm 2.8.1, vLLM at this
PR's commit
Server:
--tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 1048576 --max-num-seqs 16 --enable-prefix-caching
, speculative decoding with
num_speculative_tokens=5
. The A/B runs differ only in
VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE
(0 vs 1)
Test guards
pytest -q tests/kernels/attention/test_candidate_paged_logits.py
The tests cover:
Scores and selection:
candidate logits against an FP32 reference
(
rtol=2e-2
,
atol=1e-2
), plus selected-set comparisons for
persistent
and
auto
top-k. This is kernel-level coverage, not model accuracy.
Cache layout:
page gaps of 0/64/260 bytes with block sizes 16/64;
invalid cache entry widths are rejected.
Bounds:
empty contexts, padded/out-of-range candidate blocks, and
per-row causal limits during speculative decoding.
CUDA graphs:
capture on a short context, replay with changed lengths
and page tables, then compare against eager execution.
Gating and workspace:
default-off behavior, rejected configurations,
and reuse of the reserved workspace without growth during capture.
Performance smoke test:
an effective-bandwidth threshold over the
candidate path, intended to catch severe regressions, not to measure
isolated HBM bandwidth.
The current L4 attention CI job skips the SM90 GPU cases. A saved H20 pytest
report for the submitted revision is still needed; the coverage above does
not imply those cases passed in CI.
End-to-end A/B (1M context)
I ran both configurations on the same commit with the same client arguments.
There is one run per configuration, with 2/4/8/16 measured requests at
concurrency 1/2/4/8 respectively. Set

supporting results. Under speculative decoding, streamed chunks can contain
multiple tokens: client ITL is not necessarily one GPU iteration, nor is it
independent of acceptance, scheduling or buffering. TPOT remains a valid

so this is not a throughput win at every concurrency.
I also ran an earlier TP4 test at 200K context. It showed a much smaller ITL
change; the TP8 evalscope run and trace below are the main evidence here.

This confirms that serving actually exercises the new path.
The batches differ, so these are attribution measurements, not a matched-load
speedup. Even dividing by row count does not fully remove differences in
occupancy and batch composition. End-to-end latency comes from evalscope,
not the profiler's summed CUDA time.
Accuracy
Model-level accuracy results are pending. I'll compare the flag on and off
with lm-eval and add the results here before merge. Kernel tests alone do not
establish model accuracy. Other SM90 GPUs have not been tested.
Details
The path prepares per-row candidate blocks and causal bounds, reads candidate
K directly through the page table, scores into a compact buffer, runs the
existing top-k, and remaps the selected columns to request-local positions.
It reuses candidate preparation and remapping from vLLM's SM100 sparse path.
FP8 dot products use FP32 accumulation; invalid columns are masked and valid
column counts are passed to top-k.
For the tested model,
index_head_dim=128
,
index_n_heads=32
,
candidate_topk_blocks=2048
,
candidate_block_size=8
, and
index_topk=512
.
The compact FP32 logits buffer is
[rows, 16384]
(1.5 MiB at 24 rows).
With five speculative tokens, six decode rows represent one fully populated
request in the kernel input; this is not necessarily the client's concurrent
request count because scheduling and graph padding can change the batch.
The path requires SM90, an FP8 indexer cache, no DCP/PCP, and supported
candidate geometry. When disabled or rejected by the availability check, the
existing dispatch remains in use; existing unsupported combinations may still
raise errors. The gate has no batch-size or context-length profitability
threshold. Avoiding a K copy does not remove preparation, sorting, top-k and
remapping costs, so short-context performance still needs checking.
What's next
Accuracy:
compare lm-eval results with the flag off and on.
Performance outside 1M:
benchmark shorter contexts, small batches and
smaller real datasets to check for latency or throughput regressions.
Kernel work:
try a CUDA/CUTLASS implementation and compare it with
Triton. I'll profile scoring, candidate preparation and top-k before
deciding which part to optimize; there is no measured speedup for this yet.
I'd appreciate feedback on the implementation while I finish the accuracy and
short-workload checks. Those results still need to be confirmed before merge.
Prefill optimization is outside this PR.

Score only the candidate blocks in the SM90 DSv4.1 decode indexer
…
57b53a5
The V4.1 candidate-consuming indexers have no paged sparse scoring kernel
on SM90, so they score the whole compressed context and then mask the
logits down to the candidate blocks. With a 16K-position candidate set
against a 1M-position context that discards ~98% of the scoring.

Score the candidate positions only, reading K in place from the paged FP8
indexer cache into a compact per-row logits buffer, then remap the
selected columns back to request-local positions. The candidate-source
and pre-candidate indexers stay dense, and prefill is untouched.

The path is gated by candidate_paged_decode_available(), a predicate over
model/platform/scheduler config only: SM90, FP8 indexer cache, no
DCP/PCP, power-of-two candidate geometry, and topk within the candidate
capacity. Every input is config-fixed, so the decision is a CUDA-graph
invariant: a captured graph cannot diverge from the path chosen at
capture. The profiling run reserves the candidate workspace sized by
max_num_seqs * (1 + num_speculative_tokens), so the hot path never
requests more than was profiled. The per-row candidate preparation is a
small extra step, paid only when the path is active.

Candidates are indexed per decode row, as the dense path mask does; only
the causal lengths are shared across a request's speculative rows.

Numerics follow the decode reference: dot, relu, head weights, sum over
heads, then one dequantization multiply per column. Scoring runs on fp8
tensor cores with fp32 accumulation.

Default off behind VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE.

The candidate expansion (prepare + sort) is a deterministic function of the

short contexts no longer pay MMA work for the padded tail of the fixed-width
candidate window. The grid stays static, so this is CUDA-graph safe.

On SM90, FlashMLA's sparse decode tiles query heads by 64 (the WGMMA M dimension). A DeepSeek V4.1 TP8 rank owns only 8 heads (16 at TP4), so it pads them to 64 and spends most of the tensor-core work on padding. This adds a Triton sparse decode kernel that tiles heads by 16 with
tl.dot
(mma.sync), reads the existing packed FP8 MLA cache directly, and recovers parallelism by splitting the key set across programs, merging the partial results with log-sum-exp.
Why it is faster at small batches.
At a few decode tokens per step, FlashMLA launches roughly one CTA per token and each CTA does 64-head work for 8 real heads. This kernel launches
tokens × splits
programs, each doing 16-head work over its share of keys. The best split count depends on both token count and key width: 32 splits at ≤3 tokens fills the GPU, but by 8 tokens 8 splits wins because the merge cost and per-program gather overhead dominate.
_pick_config
encodes this measured table. At larger batches the step becomes gather/dequant-bound rather than MMA-bound, so removing the padding no longer helps and FlashMLA is kept.

Layer key width (SWA + compressed top-k)
Uses this kernel at

≤256 (SWA-only layers)

FlashMLA

index_topk=512

The gate is decode tokens per rank per step (≈ batch × (1 + spec tokens)), so the gain is limited to
low-concurrency decode
. It does not depend on context length, since sparse attention reads a fixed number of keys per token. Prefill always uses FlashMLA.
JIT warmup:

+# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
+# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright contributors to the vLLM project
+"""SM90 candidate-only scoring for the DeepSeek V4.1 two-level indexer.
+
+On SM100 the candidate-consuming indexer layers score only the candidate
+blocks published by the candidate-source layer (DeepGEMM's sparse MQA-logits
+kernels, SM100-only). On SM90 those kernels do not exist, so consumers
+currently score the whole context with the dense paged MQA-logits kernel and
+then mask the logits down to the candidate blocks, discarding ~98% of the
+scoring work at long context.
+
+This module provides the SM90 substitute for decode: gather each row's
+candidate K from the paged FP8 indexer cache into a contiguous workspace,
+score it with the existing dense (non-paged) MQA-logits kernel, run the
+usual decode top-k, and remap the selected columns back to request-local
+compressed positions. For unique valid candidates this preserves the scoring
+problem without requantizing K. Different scoring kernels and top-k tie
+breaking can still change floating-point results or the selected indices.
+"""
+
+import torch
+
+from vllm.logger import init_logger
+from vllm.model_executor.kernels.attention.dsa.sparse_mqa_logits import (
+    _sparse_topk_remap_kernel,
+    candidate_blocks_to_sparse_indices,
+    pick_sparse_block_kv,
+)
+from vllm.model_executor.layers.indexer_topk import (
+    RADIX_TOPK_WORKSPACE_SIZE,
+    get_indexer_topk,
+)
+from vllm.triton_utils import tl, triton
+from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import fp8_fp4_mqa_logits
+from vllm.v1.worker.workspace import current_workspace_manager
+
+logger = init_logger(__name__)
+
+
+@triton.jit(
+    do_not_specialize=[
+        "cache_block_stride",
+        "cache_block_size",
+        "num_cols",
+        "bt_row_repeat",
+    ]
+)
+def _gather_candidate_k_kernel(
+    kv_bytes,  # uint8 flat storage view of the paged indexer cache
+    kv_scales,  # fp32 reinterpretation of the same flat storage
+    block_table,  # [B, P] int32 per-request page table
+    sparse_indices,  # [rows, S] int32 candidate sparse-block ids
+    end,  # [rows] int32 valid candidate column count
+    out_k,  # [rows, S*SBK, D] uint8 (fp8 payload bytes)
+    out_s,  # [rows, S*SBK] fp32
+    bt_row_stride,
+    bt_col_stride,
+    bt_row_repeat,
+    si_stride,
+    cache_block_stride,  # bytes per physical cache block
+    cache_block_size,  # tokens per cache block
+    num_cols,  # S*SBK
+    SBK: tl.constexpr,  # positions per sparse block
+    D: tl.constexpr,  # head_dim
+    TILE: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    """Gather candidate K (fp8 values + fp32 scales) for one row tile.
+
+    The paged FP8 indexer cache stores per block: ``block_size * head_dim``
+    value bytes followed by ``block_size * 4`` scale bytes (one fp32 scale
+    per entry). Column j of row r scores compressed position
+    ``sparse_indices[r, j // SBK] * SBK + j % SBK``; invalid tail columns
+    (j >= end) are zero-filled so the top-k bound can simply exclude them.
+    """
+    row = tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64)
+    cols = (tl.program_id(1) * TILE + tl.arange(0, TILE)).to(tl.int64)
+    in_bounds = cols < num_cols
+    e = tl.load(end + row).to(tl.int64)
+    valid = in_bounds & (cols < e)
+
+    sb = tl.load(
+        sparse_indices + row * si_stride + cols // SBK, mask=valid, other=0
+    ).to(tl.int64)
+    pos = sb * SBK + cols % SBK
+    page = pos // cache_block_size
+    off = pos % cache_block_size
+    bt_row = row // bt_row_repeat
+    phys = tl.load(
+        block_table + bt_row * bt_row_stride + page * bt_col_stride,
+        mask=valid,
+        other=0,
+    ).to(tl.int64)
+
+    val_base = phys * cache_block_stride + off * D
+    d = tl.arange(0, D)
+    vals = tl.load(
+        kv_bytes + val_base[:, None] + d[None, :], mask=valid[:, None], other=0
+    )
+    tl.store(
+        out_k + (row * num_cols + cols)[:, None] * D + d[None, :],
+        vals,
+        mask=in_bounds[:, None],
+    )
+
+    # Scales live right after the values section of the block (fp32 each).
+    sc_idx = (phys * cache_block_stride) // 4 + (cache_block_size * D) // 4 + off
+    sc = tl.load(kv_scales + sc_idx, mask=valid, other=0.0)
+    tl.store(out_s + row * num_cols + cols, sc, mask=in_bounds)
+
+
+def gather_candidate_k_decode(
+    kv_cache: torch.Tensor,
+    block_table: torch.Tensor,
+    sparse_indices: torch.Tensor,
+    end: torch.Tensor,
+    head_dim: int,
+    sparse_block_kv: int,
+    out_k: torch.Tensor,
+    out_s: torch.Tensor,
+) -> None:
+    """Gather candidate K for decode rows from the paged FP8 indexer cache."""
+    rows, num_cols = out_s.shape
+    assert kv_cache.dtype == torch.uint8 and kv_cache.ndim == 3
+    assert block_table.dtype == torch.int32 and block_table.ndim == 2
+    assert sparse_indices.dtype == torch.int32 and end.dtype == torch.int32
+    cache_block_size = kv_cache.shape[1]
+    page_bytes = cache_block_size * (head_dim + 4)
+    assert kv_cache.shape[2] == head_dim + 4, (
+        "FP8 indexer cache entry must be head_dim+4 bytes, "
+        f"got shape {tuple(kv_cache.shape)} with head_dim={head_dim}"
+    )
+    assert kv_cache.stride(2) == 1 and kv_cache.stride(0) >= page_bytes
+    assert kv_cache.storage_offset() % 4 == 0 and kv_cache.stride(0) % 4 == 0
+    assert block_table.stride(1) > 0
+    assert rows % block_table.shape[0] == 0
+    bt_row_repeat = rows // block_table.shape[0]
+
+    # Packed KV-cache views have gaps between logical pages (other layers share
+    # the same physical manager block), so ``view(-1)`` is invalid. Build a
+    # zero-copy one-dimensional storage view that includes those gaps and use
+    # the physical block stride in the kernel.
+    storage_span = (kv_cache.shape[0] - 1) * kv_cache.stride(0) + page_bytes
+    kv_bytes = torch.as_strided(kv_cache, (storage_span,), (1,))
+    assert storage_span % 4 == 0
+    _gather_candidate_k_kernel[(rows, triton.cdiv(num_cols, 64))](
+        kv_bytes,
+        kv_bytes.view(torch.float32),
+        block_table,
+        sparse_indices,
+        end,
+        out_k,
+        out_s,
+        block_table.stride(0),
+        block_table.stride(1),
+        bt_row_repeat,
+        sparse_indices.stride(0),
+        kv_cache.stride(0),
+        cache_block_size,
+        num_cols,
+        SBK=sparse_block_kv,
+        D=head_dim,
+        TILE=64,
+        num_warps=4,
+    )
+
+
+@triton.jit
+def _prepare_candidate_rows_kernel(
+    seq_lens,
+    row_ks,
+    row_ends,
+    col_starts,
+    rows,
+    next_n: tl.constexpr,
+    num_cols: tl.constexpr,
+    per_row_lens: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
+    mask = offsets < rows
+    if per_row_lens:
+        lens = tl.load(seq_lens + offsets, mask=mask, other=0)
+    else:
+        request = offsets // next_n
+        step = offsets % next_n
+        base = tl.load(seq_lens + request, mask=mask, other=0)
+        lens = tl.maximum(base - next_n + 1 + step, 0)
+    tl.store(row_ks + offsets, 0, mask=mask)
+    tl.store(row_ends + offsets, lens, mask=mask)
+    tl.store(col_starts + offsets, offsets * num_cols, mask=mask)
+
+
+def candidate_gather_workspace_specs(
+    rows: int,
+    num_candidates: int,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    head_dim: int,
+    topk_tokens: int,
+) -> list[tuple[tuple[int, ...], torch.dtype]]:
+    """Simultaneously-live scratch for candidate-only decode scoring.
+
+    The radix reservation must stay first: nested cooperative/persistent top-k
+    requests the same workspace prefix while the remaining buffers are live.
+    """
+    sparse_block_kv = pick_sparse_block_kv(candidate_block_size)
+    ratio = candidate_block_size // sparse_block_kv
+    assert ratio in (1, 2) and ratio * sparse_block_kv == candidate_block_size
+    num_cols = num_candidates * candidate_block_size
+    num_sparse = num_candidates * ratio
+    return [
+        ((RADIX_TOPK_WORKSPACE_SIZE,), torch.uint8),
+        ((rows,), torch.int32),  # row_ks
+        ((rows, num_sparse), torch.int32),
+        ((rows,), torch.int32),  # row_ends, then candidate-column ends
+        ((rows, num_cols, head_dim), torch.uint8),
+        ((rows, num_cols), torch.float32),
+        ((rows,), torch.int32),  # flattened candidate-row starts
+        ((rows,), torch.int32),  # flattened candidate-row ends
+        ((rows, topk_tokens), torch.int32),
+    ]
+
+
+def candidate_gather_score_decode(
+    q: torch.Tensor,
+    kv_cache: torch.Tensor,
+    weights: torch.Tensor,
+    seq_lens: torch.Tensor,
+    block_table: torch.Tensor,
+    candidate_blocks: torch.Tensor,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    next_n: int,
+    topk_tokens: int,
+    topk_backend: str,
+    topk_indices: torch.Tensor,
+    head_dim: int,
+    max_seq_len: int,
+    fp8_dtype: torch.dtype,
+) -> None:
+    """Score only candidate blocks for decode rows (SM90 substitute for the
+    SM100 sparse MQA-logits path) and write request-local top-k indices.
+
+    Args:
+        q: [rows, H, D] fp8 query values (per-token scale folded into
+            ``weights`` on the SM90 FP8 path). Rows follow the padded decode
+            layout ``[B, next_n]`` flattened.
+        kv_cache: [num_blocks, block_size, head_dim + 4] uint8 indexer cache.
+        weights: [rows, H] per-head weights.
+        seq_lens: [B, next_n] or [B, 1] int32 per-row effective context lens.
+        block_table: [rows, P] int32 per-row page table.
+        candidate_blocks: [rows, K] int32 candidate block ids (-1 padded), in
+            units of ``candidate_block_size`` compressed positions. K must be
+            a power of two.
+        candidate_block_size: Compressed positions per candidate block.
+        next_n: Query rows per request in the padded layout.
+        topk_tokens: Number of tokens to keep per row.
+        topk_backend: Decode top-k backend (see ``get_indexer_topk``).
+        topk_indices: [rows, topk_tokens] int32 output buffer.
+        head_dim: Indexer head dim.
+        max_seq_len: Host-side maximum context length for this batch.
+        fp8_dtype: The platform FP8 dtype for the K workspace.
+
+    """
+    rows = q.shape[0]
+    num_candidates = candidate_blocks.shape[1]
+    assert candidate_blocks.dtype == torch.int32
+    assert block_table.shape[0] in (rows, rows // next_n)
+    assert candidate_blocks.shape[0] in (rows, rows // next_n)
+    sparse_block_kv = pick_sparse_block_kv(candidate_block_size)
+    num_cols = num_candidates * candidate_block_size
+
+    (
+        _radix_reserve,
+        row_ks,
+        sparse_indices,
+        end,
+        k_gathered,

+def candidate_gather_decode_profitable(
+    max_seq_len: int,
+    num_rows: int,
+    num_candidates: int,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+) -> bool:
+    """Apply user-tunable host-side shape gates before candidate scoring.
+
+    Dense scoring reads the whole context for every decode row, while
+    candidate scoring reads a fixed candidate width per row and is dominated
+    by a per-step fixed cost. The crossover therefore tracks the scanned work
+    ``num_rows * max_seq_len`` relative to the candidate width, not the
+    context length alone. The crossover constant is hardware-dependent, so no
+    device-specific value is baked in here.
+    """
+    import vllm.envs as envs
+
+    if envs.VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_FORCE:
+        return True
+
+    candidate_width = num_candidates * candidate_block_size
+    min_ratio = max(1, envs.VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_WORK_RATIO)
+    min_rows = max(1, envs.VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_MIN_ROWS)

+        return False
+    return num_rows * max_seq_len >= min_ratio * candidate_width

+def candidate_gather_decode_available(
+    use_fp4_cache: bool,
+    dcp_world_size: int,
+    use_pcp: bool,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    num_candidates: int,
+    topk_tokens: int,
+    topk_backend: str,
+) -> bool:
+    """Whether the SM90 gather-based candidate scoring path applies.
+
+    Restricted to SM90 FP8-cache decode without context parallelism; SM100
+    has the native sparse kernels and other platforms keep the dense
+    score-then-mask fallback.
+    """
+    import vllm.envs as envs
+    from vllm.platforms import current_platform
+    from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import has_deep_gemm
+
+    if not envs.VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_GATHER_DECODE:
+        return False
+    if not (
+        current_platform.is_cuda() and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(90)
+    ):
+        return False
+    if use_fp4_cache or dcp_world_size != 1 or use_pcp:
+        return False
+    if topk_backend == "deep_select":
+        return False
+    if not has_deep_gemm():
+        return False
+    if num_candidates <= 0 or num_candidates & (num_candidates - 1):
+        # The candidate-expansion kernel's in-register sort needs pow2.
+        return False
+    if candidate_block_size <= 0 or topk_tokens > num_candidates * candidate_block_size:
+        return False
+    try:
+        sparse_block_kv = pick_sparse_block_kv(candidate_block_size)
+    except ValueError:
+        return False
+    ratio = candidate_block_size // sparse_block_kv
+    return ratio in (1, 2) and ratio * sparse_block_kv == candidate_block_size

+# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright contributors to the vLLM project
+"""SM90 candidate-only decode scoring for the DeepSeek V4.1 two-level indexer.
+
+The V4.1 indexer publishes candidate blocks at ``candidate_source_layer_id``;
+the later consumer indexers are meant to select their top-k *inside those
+candidate blocks only*. On SM100 that is DeepGEMM's sparse MQA-logits kernels.
+SM90 has no equivalent, so the consumers score the whole compressed context
+with the dense paged kernel and then mask the logits down to the candidate
+blocks, discarding the work outside them. With a 16K-position candidate set
+against a 1M-position context that is ~98% of the scoring.
+
+This module scores only the candidate positions, reading K **in place** from
+the paged FP8 indexer cache. Logits land in a compact ``[rows, num_cands *
+candidate_block_size]`` buffer whose columns are candidate-relative, the usual
+decode top-k runs over that buffer, and the selected columns are remapped back
+to request-local compressed positions.
+
+Two properties keep replays correct under full CUDA-graph capture:
+
+* **No per-step host decision.** Context lengths stay on the device; the host
+  only sees shapes that are fixed by the model and scheduler config. A full
+  CUDA graph therefore cannot bake a context-dependent choice, and replays
+  stay correct at any live context length.
+* **K is read in place.** Unlike a scheme that gathers candidate K into a
+  scratch buffer first, no K data is copied that the dense path would not
+  also read. The only extra work is per-row candidate bookkeeping (expansion
+  and sorting of block ids), index arithmetic paid only while the path is
+  active.
+
+Numerics follow the decode reference (``fp8_paged_mqa_logits``): dot, relu,
+head weights, sum over heads, then one dequantization multiply per column.
+Scaling after the relu is exact because the per-position scale is positive,
+and it costs ``num_heads`` times fewer multiplies.

+from vllm.model_executor.kernels.attention.dsa.sparse_mqa_logits import (
+    _sparse_topk_remap_kernel,

+)

+    RADIX_TOPK_WORKSPACE_SIZE,
+    get_indexer_topk,
+)

+    per_row_lens: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    """Per-row causal context length, and the zero K-range start the paged
+    candidate expansion expects (its block ids are context-relative)."""
+    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
+    mask = offsets < rows
+    if per_row_lens:
+        lens = tl.load(seq_lens + offsets, mask=mask, other=0)
+    else:
+        # One length per request: speculative row ``s`` of a request sees
+        # ``next_n - 1 - s`` fewer positions than the request's newest row.
+        request = offsets // next_n
+        step = offsets % next_n
+        base = tl.load(seq_lens + request, mask=mask, other=0)
+        lens = tl.maximum(base - next_n + 1 + step, 0)
+    tl.store(row_ks + offsets, 0, mask=mask)
+    tl.store(row_ends + offsets, lens, mask=mask)
+
+
+@triton.jit(
+    # ``cache_block_stride`` and ``cache_block_size`` are deliberately left
+    # specializable: Triton needs their divisibility to prove that a
+    # position's value bytes are 16-byte aligned and emit vector loads for the
+    # candidate gather. Hiding it costs roughly 20x on the K stream.
+    do_not_specialize=[
+        "num_blocks",
+        "bt_width",
+        "width",
+        "bt_row_repeat",
+    ]
+)
+def _paged_candidate_logits_kernel(
+    q_ptr,  # fp8 [rows, H, D]
+    kv_bytes,  # uint8 flat storage view of the paged indexer cache
+    kv_scales,  # fp32 reinterpretation of the same flat storage
+    w_ptr,  # fp32 [rows, H]
+    blocks_ptr,  # int32 [rows, S] candidate block ids, sorted, padded tail
+    end_ptr,  # int32 [rows] valid compact column count
+    causal_ptr,  # int32 [rows] causal context length, compressed positions
+    bt_ptr,  # int32 [bt_rows, P] page table
+    out_ptr,  # fp32 [rows, width]
+    stride_q_row,
+    stride_q_head,
+    stride_w_row,
+    stride_blocks_row,
+    stride_bt_row,
+    stride_bt_col,
+    stride_out_row,
+    bt_row_repeat,
+    cache_block_stride,  # bytes per physical cache block
+    cache_block_size,  # positions per cache block
+    num_blocks,
+    bt_width,
+    width,
+    H: tl.constexpr,  # indexer heads actually present
+    H_PAD: tl.constexpr,  # padded to a power of two for the MMA
+    D: tl.constexpr,  # indexer head dim
+    CBS: tl.constexpr,  # positions per candidate block
+    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr,  # compact columns per program
+):
+    """Score one tile of candidate columns for one decode row.
+
+    Compact column ``c`` scores request-local compressed position
+    ``blocks[row, c // CBS] * CBS + c % CBS``. Columns past the row's valid
+    candidate prefix, columns whose block is padding, and columns past the
+    row's causal length all become ``-inf`` so the top-k never selects them.
+    """
+    row = tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64)
+    cols = tl.program_id(1) * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
+    in_bounds = cols < width
+
+    end = tl.load(end_ptr + row)
+    causal = tl.load(causal_ptr + row)
+    live = in_bounds & (cols < end)
+
+    blk = tl.load(
+        blocks_ptr + row * stride_blocks_row + cols // CBS, mask=live, other=-1
+    ).to(tl.int64)
+    pos = blk * CBS + cols % CBS
+    # The expansion pads the tail with a repeat of the largest block, so the
+    # causal bound is what rejects those columns.
+    live = live & (blk >= 0) & (pos < causal)
+
+    page = tl.where(live, pos // cache_block_size, 0)
+    live = live & (page < bt_width)
+    phys = tl.load(
+        bt_ptr + (row // bt_row_repeat) * stride_bt_row + page * stride_bt_col,
+        mask=live,
+        other=-1,
+    ).to(tl.int64)
+    live = live & (phys >= 0) & (phys < num_blocks)
+    safe_phys = tl.where(live, phys, 0)
+    page_off = tl.where(live, pos % cache_block_size, 0)
+
+    d = tl.arange(0, D)
+    h = tl.arange(0, H_PAD)
+    h_live = h < H
+
+    # Values are contiguous per position, so a column's D bytes are one
+    # coalesced segment and consecutive columns of a candidate block adjoin.
+    k_offset = safe_phys * cache_block_stride + page_off * D
+    k_block = tl.load(
+        kv_bytes + k_offset[:, None] + d[None, :],
+        mask=live[:, None],
+        other=0,
+    ).to(tl.float8e4nv, bitcast=True)
+    # Zero-padded heads contribute relu(0) * 0 = 0, so the padding is exact.
+    # Loaded as the MMA's K-major operand directly; the tile is small and this
+    # avoids an in-kernel transpose of an fp8 operand.
+    q_block = tl.load(
+        q_ptr + row * stride_q_row + h[None, :] * stride_q_head + d[:, None],
+        mask=h_live[None, :],
+        other=0.0,
+    )
+    weights = tl.load(w_ptr + row * stride_w_row + h, mask=h_live, other=0.0).to(
+        tl.float32
+    )
+
+    # [BLOCK_N, H_PAD] on fp8 tensor cores with fp32 accumulation. Scoring the
+    # columns as the MMA's M dimension keeps the large operand untransposed.
+    scores = tl.dot(k_block, q_block)
+    scores = tl.maximum(scores, 0.0)
+    scores = scores * weights[None, :]
+    acc = tl.sum(scores, axis=1)
+
+    # Scales follow the block's value bytes, one fp32 per position.
+    sc_idx = (
+        (safe_phys * cache_block_stride) // _SCALE_BYTES
+        + (cache_block_size * D) // _SCALE_BYTES
+        + page_off
+    )
+    acc = acc * tl.load(kv_scales + sc_idx, mask=live, other=0.0)
+
+    tl.store(
+        out_ptr + row * stride_out_row + cols,
+        tl.where(live, acc, -float("inf")),
+        mask=in_bounds,
+    )
+

+def _flat_cache_views(
+    kv_cache: torch.Tensor, head_dim: int
+) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
+    """Zero-copy ``(uint8, fp32)`` one-dimensional views of the cache storage.
+
+    Packed KV-cache views leave gaps between logical pages, because other
+    layers share the same physical manager block, so ``view(-1)`` is invalid.
+    Span the gaps instead and let the kernel use the physical block stride.
+    """
+    cache_block_size = kv_cache.shape[1]
+    page_bytes = cache_block_size * (head_dim + INDEXER_SCALE_BYTES)
+    assert kv_cache.dtype == torch.uint8 and kv_cache.ndim == 3
+    assert kv_cache.shape[2] == head_dim + INDEXER_SCALE_BYTES, (
+        "FP8 indexer cache entry must be head_dim+4 bytes, got shape "
+        f"{tuple(kv_cache.shape)} with head_dim={head_dim}"
+    )
+    assert kv_cache.stride(2) == 1 and kv_cache.stride(0) >= page_bytes
+    assert kv_cache.storage_offset() % INDEXER_SCALE_BYTES == 0
+    assert kv_cache.stride(0) % INDEXER_SCALE_BYTES == 0
+    storage_span = (kv_cache.shape[0] - 1) * kv_cache.stride(0) + page_bytes
+    assert storage_span % INDEXER_SCALE_BYTES == 0
+    kv_bytes = torch.as_strided(kv_cache, (storage_span,), (1,))
+    return kv_bytes, kv_bytes.view(torch.float32)
+
+
+def paged_candidate_logits(
+    q: torch.Tensor,
+    kv_cache: torch.Tensor,
+    weights: torch.Tensor,
+    candidate_blocks: torch.Tensor,
+    end: torch.Tensor,
+    causal_lens: torch.Tensor,
+    block_table: torch.Tensor,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    head_dim: int,
+    out: torch.Tensor,
+) -> None:
+    """Score each row's candidate positions into a compact logits buffer.
+
+    Args:
+        q: [rows, H, D] fp8 queries. On the SM90 FP8 path the per-token scale
+            is already folded into ``weights``.
+        kv_cache: [num_blocks, block_size, head_dim + 4] uint8 paged indexer
+            cache; per block, all value bytes then all fp32 scales.
+        weights: [rows, H] per-head weights.
+        candidate_blocks: [rows, S] int32 candidate block ids, sorted with a
+            padded tail, as produced by ``candidate_blocks_to_sparse_indices``.
+        end: [rows] int32 valid compact column count per row.
+        causal_lens: [rows] int32 causal context length in compressed
+            positions.
+        block_table: [bt_rows, P] int32 page table; ``rows`` must be a whole
+            multiple of ``bt_rows`` for speculative row expansion.
+        candidate_block_size: Compressed positions per candidate block.
+        head_dim: Indexer head dim.
+        out: [rows, S * candidate_block_size] fp32 output.

+    num_heads = q.shape[1]

+    assert q.shape[2] == head_dim

+    assert candidate_blocks.shape[0] == rows
+    assert candidate_blocks.shape[1] * candidate_block_size == width
+    assert candidate_blocks.dtype == torch.int32
+    assert end.dtype == torch.int32 and causal_lens.dtype == torch.int32
+    assert block_table.dtype == torch.int32 and block_table.ndim == 2
+    assert rows % block_table.shape[0] == 0
+    assert q.stride(2) == 1

+    block_n = max(_BLOCK_N, candidate_block_size)
+    assert block_n % candidate_block_size == 0

+        q,
+        kv_bytes,
+        kv_scales,
+        weights,
+        candidate_blocks,
+        end,
+        causal_lens,
+        block_table,
+        out,
+        q.stride(0),
+        q.stride(1),
+        weights.stride(0),
+        candidate_blocks.stride(0),
+        block_table.stride(0),
+        block_table.stride(1),
+        out.stride(0),
+        rows // block_table.shape[0],
+        kv_cache.stride(0),
+        kv_cache.shape[1],
+        kv_cache.shape[0],
+        block_table.shape[1],
+        width,
+        H=num_heads,
+        H_PAD=triton.next_power_of_2(num_heads),
+        D=head_dim,
+        CBS=candidate_block_size,
+        BLOCK_N=block_n,
+    )
+
+
+def candidate_paged_workspace_specs(
+    rows: int,
+    num_candidates: int,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    topk_tokens: int,

+    """Simultaneously-live scratch for candidate-only decode scoring.

+        end.view(-1, next_n),

+def candidate_paged_decode_available(
+    use_fp4_cache: bool,
+    dcp_world_size: int,
+    use_pcp: bool,
+    candidate_block_size: int,
+    num_candidates: int,
+    topk_tokens: int,
+    head_dim: int,
+) -> bool:
+    """Whether candidate-only decode scoring applies to this configuration.
+
+    Every input is fixed by the model, platform and scheduler config, so the
+    answer is a CUDA-graph invariant: a captured graph cannot diverge from the
+    path chosen while it was captured.
+
+    Restricted to SM90 with the FP8 indexer cache and no context parallelism.
+    SM100 has the native sparse kernels, and the other platforms keep the
+    dense score-then-mask fallback.
+    """
+    import vllm.envs as envs
+    from vllm.platforms import current_platform
+
+    if not envs.VLLM_DSA_CANDIDATE_PAGED_DECODE:
+        return False
+    if not (
+        current_platform.is_cuda() and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(90)
+    ):

+        return False

+        return False
+    if candidate_block_size <= 0 or candidate_block_size & (candidate_block_size - 1):

+        # whole number of candidate blocks.
+        return False

+        return False
+    # The MMA's K dimension is the head dim.
+    return head_dim > 0 and not (head_dim & (head_dim - 1))

Summary
This PR adds an opt-in, two-stage packed selected-KV sparse decode path for the
GLM-5.2 / V3.2 FP8 MLA format on SM90:
pack_selected_kv
gathers selected records from the paged KV cache into an
opaque tile-major workspace.
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
consumes that workspace with a packed
sparse-decode specialization that avoids sparse index and page translation
on the attention critical path.
The existing native sparse-decode API and dispatch remain unchanged. The new
path is explicitly restricted to SM90 and is not enabled automatically.
Note
Alternative host-offload path (not part of this pr):
The packed interface also enables a separate offload path in which gathering and packing are performed on the host, followed by transferring only the packed selected-KV workspace to the device. In this case, the full KV caches of the shared layers no longer need to remain resident in HBM. This can substantially expand KV-cache capacity.
Since this implementation introduces a compile-time packed-KV specialization in the existing SM90 sparse decode kernel, I’d appreciate maintainers’ guidance on whether you prefer the current shared-kernel approach, a policy/loader-based abstraction, or a separate packed-kernel implementation; I’m happy to restructure it in a follow-up revision based on your feedback.
Motivation
GLM-5.2 can share selected physical indices across multiple MLA layers. When
those indices are available before the layer that consumes them, the runtime
can move sparse address resolution and KV gathering into an earlier overlap
window.
The attention kernel can then read a contiguous packed workspace instead of
repeatedly:
loading and validating physical indices;
translating indices into page and in-page coordinates;
constructing unrelated global addresses; and
gathering NoPE, scale, and RoPE components from the paged cache.
Packing and attention are intentionally separate operations so a runtime can
overlap packing with preceding work such as MoE communication.
What changed
SM90 packing kernel
pack_selected_kv
copies each selected 656-byte V3.2 record byte-for-byte:
512-byte FP8 E4M3 NoPE data;
16-byte FP32 scales; and
128-byte BF16 RoPE data.
The packer writes an opaque 64-token tile-major workspace. It supports a valid
selected-index prefix described by
topk_length
and zero-fills invalid suffix
records.
Callers may provide reusable contiguous
uint8
storage using
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
.
Packed attention specialization
The packed H=64 and H=128 instantiations reuse FlashMLA's existing:
WGMMA and dequantization pipeline;
online softmax;
DSM clustering for H=128;
split accumulation;
epilogue; and
combine kernel.
The specialization replaces the sparse index/page/gather loader with direct
tile-major loads and preserves partial-tail masking.
Scheduler policy
H=128 uses the same scheduler as native sparse decode.
H=64 uses the compact request-local scheduler selected by the L20X
experiments. For the measured full-prefix
topk=2048
, 132-SM
B*S_q=16
regime, it falls back to the faster native scheduler.
This scheduler is used only by the opt-in packed helper and does not change
native sparse decode. The benchmark includes an identical-scheduler control to
isolate the packed-load kernel gain.
Python API
This PR adds:
get_packed_kv_workspace_size
get_packed_mla_metadata
pack_selected_kv
flash_mla_with_packed_kvcache
Supported scope
The initial path is intentionally limited to:
SM90;
V3.2 FP8 sparse KV records;
d_qk=576
;
d_v=512
;
H in {64, 128}
;
MQA KV; and
top-k capacity divisible by 64.
The API fails closed for unsupported architectures and shapes. SM100 is not
enabled because this implementation has only been evaluated on SM90.
L20X results
The repository-local benchmark was run on an NVIDIA L20X with 132 SMs using:
CUDA 13.0;
PyTorch 2.13.0;
topk=2048
;
B={1,2,4,7,8}

;

request-disjoint physical KV ranges;
a 512 MiB L2 flush before each measured path;
10 warmups and 200 timed repetitions; and
60 total cases.

The unhidden result is included deliberately: this path is useful only when
the runtime can move most packing work outside the attention critical path.
This PR does not add automatic dispatch or change the default native path.
The H=64 hybrid policy selected the tuned scheduler in 26 cases and the native
fallback in four cases. The four fallback cases improved by approximately
6.5% to 7.4% compared with using the tuned scheduler unconditionally.
Correctness and benchmark coverage

  --output packed_sparse_decode_latency.csv
The correctness test passes five cases covering:
a single full boundary tile;
H=64 partial tails and heterogeneous active lengths;
the H=64 native-scheduler fallback;
full production top-k with H=128; and
H=128 heterogeneous partial tails.
The tests compare both output and LSE with native sparse decode and verify the

Observed result:

The new CUDA kernels compiled for SM90 without register spills. The packer

Runtime follow-up
This PR contains the two FlashMLA kernels needed for the packed path, but
intentionally does not include current-token runtime orchestration.
A future vLLM integration can:
pack historical records early into caller-managed storage;
overwrite any selected current-token record after its KV becomes available,
for example with a scatter operation;
synchronize the packing/update stream with attention; and
select native fallback when the expected overlap is insufficient.
Workspace pooling, CUDA stream placement, current-token updates, overlap
eligibility, and end-to-end TPOT measurements belong to that runtime
integration.
For

so runtime dispatch should also enforce a workspace budget.
Non-goals
This PR does not:

enable the packed path by default;
add SM100 support;
claim an end-to-end speedup without concurrent runtime integration; or

MISA: Mixture of Indexer Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference



Ruijie Zhou

  
Fanxu Meng11footnotemark: 
 1
 
 
 
 

  
Yufei Xu

  
Tongxuan Liu

Muhan Zhang

  
Wenjie Pei
††thanks: Corresponding author: fxmeng@stu.pku.edu.cn, wenjiecoder@outlook.com.
Affiliation:  https://github.com/MuLabPKU/TransArch https://github.com/MuLabPKU/TransArch



Abstract
 

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) sets the state of the art for fine-grained inference-time sparse attention by introducing a learned token-wise indexer that scores every prefix token and selects the top-kk for the main attention. To remain expressive, the indexer uses HIH^{I} query heads (e.g. 6464 on DeepSeek-V3.2) that share the same selected token set; this multi-head design is precisely what makes the indexer the dominant cost on long contexts. We propose MISA (Mixture of Indexer Sparse Attention), a drop-in replacement for the DSA indexer that treats its HIH^{I} heads as a pool of mixture-of-experts: a lightweight router uses cheap block-level statistics to pick a query-dependent subset of h≪HIh\ll H^{I} active heads, and only those heads run the heavy token-level scoring. This preserves the diversity of the original indexer pool while reducing the per-query cost from 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L) to 𝒪⁡(h​L+HI​M)\mathcal{O}(hL+H^{I}M) with M=⌈L/B⌉≪LM=\lceil L/B\rceil\ll L pooled keys. Following HISA, we further introduce a hierarchical variant, MISA†, that uses the MoE-routed pass to keep an enlarged candidate set and then re-ranks it with the original DSA indexer to recover the final top-kk almost exactly. With h=8h=8 active heads and no additional training, MISA matches the dense DSA indexer on LongBench across DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 while running with 8×8\times and 4×4\times fewer indexer heads, respectively, and outperforms HISA on average; it preserves fully green Needle-in-a-Haystack heatmaps up to 128K context and recovers more than 92%92\% of the tokens selected by the DSA indexer per layer. Our TileLang kernel delivers roughly a 3.82×3.82\times speedup over DSA’s original indexer kernel on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. These results show that indexer-head-axis routing is a practical and complementary axis of efficiency for fine-grained sparse attention, on top of the existing token-axis hierarchies.
 



1 Introduction







(a) DSA



(b) MISA

Figure 1: Comparison of the DSA and MISA indexers. (a) DSA scores every prefix token with all HIH^{I} indexer heads in parallel before the Top-kk Selector picks the final tokens. (b) MISA introduces a lightweight Router that uses block-pooled indexing keys 𝐤~bI\tilde{\mathbf{k}}_{b}^{I} (cf. Eq. 4) to choose a query-dependent subset of h≪HIh\ll H^{I} active heads, and only those heads compute the per-token score. Both designs feed the same Sparse Multi-Head Latent Attention operator and produce a top-kk token set of identical size, so MISA is a drop-in replacement for the DSA indexer.




Frontier large language models such as Qwen3 [25], Kimi K2 [18], GLM-5 [28], and DeepSeek-V3.2 [7] now routinely process prefixes of hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single forward pass, and the latest releases—GPT-5.5 [19], Claude Opus 4.7 [1], Gemini 3 [11], MiniMax-01 [15], and DeepSeek-V4 [8]—push this to the million-token regime. At these lengths, dense attention becomes the dominant cost of both prefill and decode, motivating a wave of sparse attention techniques that select only a small subset 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} of past tokens for each query position [5, 3, 27, 23, 30, 16, 21, 22, 4, 10, 17, 26, 24]. Among them, DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) [7] stands out as the best-performing fine-grained variant in production: rather than selecting whole blocks of tokens with handcrafted patterns, DSA introduces a lightweight learned indexer that scores every prefix token and feeds the top-kk tokens into the main attention. Its dominance carries into the next generation: DeepSeek-V4’s Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) [8] is, at its core, DSA applied on top of a 4×4\times compressed (block-level) KV stream, confirming that learned token-wise indexing remains the strongest building block even when the underlying KV is itself compressed. By contrast, block-level inference-time alternatives such as MoBA [17] consistently lag behind DSA on retrieval-style benchmarks because their per-block scores cannot localise the relevant content within a block.




A central design choice of DSA is that the indexer itself is multi-head: although the main attention in DeepSeek-V3.2 has H=128H=128 query heads, all of them share the same selected token set 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} (the sparse MLA operates in MQA mode with a single key/value entry per token), so a single indexer is sufficient—yet DSA still uses HI=64H^{I}=64 indexer heads. The reason is expressiveness: each head specialises in a different relevance pattern (recency, syntactic role, lexical or semantic similarity, …), and the aggregated score It,s=∑jwt,jI​ReLU​(𝐪t,jI⋅𝐤sI)I_{t,s}=\sum_{j}w_{t,j}^{I}\,\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{I}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{k}_{s}^{I}) benefits from this diversity, with measurable retrieval degradation as HIH^{I} shrinks. The unfortunate consequence is that scoring each of the LL prefix tokens with all HIH^{I} heads is precisely what makes the indexer the dominant cost on long contexts. Two recent improvements try to reduce this indexer cost without touching the head axis. IndexCache [2] retains only a small set of layers as full indexer layers and lets the remaining shared layers reuse their top-kk, amortising the cost across layers; HISA [24] attacks the cost from the token axis with a hierarchical block-to-token search. Both still keep every one of the HIH^{I} heads active inside the kernel, and both step away from DSA’s strict per-token, per-layer scoring—tokens outside HISA’s selected blocks and entire shared layers in IndexCache no longer receive a fresh fine-grained score, sacrificing part of the granularity that makes DSA strong.




This paper takes the orthogonal view that the bottleneck is the head axis. Our key observation is that, while diversity across heads is essential when aggregated over a large pool, only a few heads are actually informative for any given query: the relevant set changes slowly along the prefix and can be identified from cheap block-level statistics. We turn this observation into MISA (Mixture of Indexer Sparse Attention), an indexer that treats the HIH^{I} heads as a pool of MoE experts, routes a query-dependent subset of h≪HIh\ll H^{I} active heads via a block-pooled scorer, and runs the heavy token-level scan with only those heads. The router itself operates on M=⌈L/B⌉≪LM=\lceil L/B\rceil\ll L pooled keys, so its overhead is negligible, and the per-query indexer cost is reduced from 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L) to 𝒪⁡(h​L+HI​M)\mathcal{O}(hL+H^{I}M). MISA preserves the full diversity of the indexer pool because every head remains available; routing simply chooses which ones to consult on each token. We further show that MISA can be plugged into a coarse-to-fine pipeline (MISA†) that uses an enlarged routed candidate set followed by a token-level DSA refinement, recovering the dense indexer’s selections almost exactly.


Contributions.




(i) We identify the indexer’s per-token head–token products as the dominant cost of DSA on long contexts and introduce head-axis routing as an axis of efficiency that is complementary to the token-axis hierarchies explored by HISA [24] and block-level methods [17, 21, 22]. (ii) We propose MISA, a drop-in MoE-routed indexer that activates only h≪HIh\ll H^{I} heads per query through a lightweight block-pooled router, and a hierarchical extension MISA† that re-ranks a routed candidate set with the original DSA indexer to recover the dense top-kk almost exactly. (iii) Without any additional training, MISA matches the dense DSA indexer on LongBench within 0.50.5 average points across DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 while running with h=8h=8 active heads (8×8\times and 4×4\times fewer indexer heads, respectively), preserves full Needle-in-a-Haystack accuracy up to 128K context, and recovers more than 92%92\% of the tokens selected by the DSA indexer per layer on LSHT. (iv) Our TileLang kernel implementation delivers roughly a 3.82×3.82\times speedup over DSA’s original indexer kernel on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Together, these results show that head-level routing is a practical efficiency axis for fine-grained sparse attention, on top of any existing token-level scheme.





2 Related work


Sparse attention.




A long line of work attacks the quadratic cost of attention on long contexts by selecting a subset of past tokens for each query. Static-pattern methods such as Sparse Transformer [5], Longformer [3], and BigBird [27] use predefined window, stride, and global tokens that are decoupled from the actual content. Cache-eviction methods drop tokens at decode time using attention-statistics heuristics: StreamingLLM [23] keeps a few attention sinks plus a recent window, H2O [30] retains heavy hitters in past attention, and SnapKV [16] clusters and compresses the KV cache. These methods avoid retrieval entirely and can therefore lose information that becomes relevant later in the generation.




A more recent class of methods uses content-based dynamic retrieval at the block level. Quest [21] and InfLLM [22] score blocks of tokens by their pooled key against the query and select the top-mm blocks at decode time. MoBA [17] extends this idea to a trained inference-time selector with the same block-level granularity. MagicPIG [4] replaces top-kk retrieval with LSH-based importance sampling. SeerAttention [10] learns a sparse gate jointly with the model. Native Sparse Attention [26] is the first work to train a transformer with a hardware-aligned sparsity pattern from scratch. Among inference-time methods, DeepSeek Sparse Attention [7] is currently the strongest: a learned token-wise indexer scores every prefix token (rather than every block), and the resulting top-kk matches dense attention quality at production scale. HISA [24] accelerates the DSA indexer with a coarse-to-fine block-to-token search, and IndexCache [2] amortises the same indexer across consecutive layers by retaining only a few full indexer layers and reusing their top-kk in the rest; both still keep every indexer head active inside the kernel and depart from per-token, per-layer scoring. MISA is complementary to all of these works: instead of acting along the token axis, we route along the head axis of the indexer itself, which can be combined orthogonally with any token-level scheme.



Mixture of experts in language models.




Conditional computation via mixture of experts (MoE) was introduced by Shazeer et al. [20] and scaled up in GShard [14] and Switch Transformer [9], where a learned router activates a sparse subset of expert FFNs per token. Modern open-weight LLMs such as Mixtral [12] and DeepSeek-MoE [6] make their FFN layers MoE-based while leaving the attention layers dense. Attention-side MoE has also been explored: Mixture-of-Attention-Heads [29] treats whole multi-head attention modules as experts and routes one module per token; MoH [13] treats each individual attention head as an expert and selects a sparse subset of heads to compute the attention output. MISA adopts the same head-as-expert philosophy as MoH but applies it to a fundamentally different module. MoH and prior attention MoEs route the heads that produce the attention output, so changing the routed subset directly changes the values written back into the residual stream. MISA instead routes the heads that produce the indexer score: the routed subset only decides which similarity patterns are consulted when picking the top-kk tokens, while the downstream attention itself remains dense over the chosen set.This decoupling is what makes it possible to use a very small number of experts (h≪HIh\ll H^{I}) without harming model quality.





3 Preliminaries




We briefly review DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) as used in DeepSeek-V3.2 [7] and a follow-up indexer-side improvement, HISA [24]; both serve as baselines and as the starting points for the design of MISA. DSA consists of two components: a token-wise indexer that selects a small set of relevant tokens for each query, and Sparse MLA that performs attention only over the selected tokens. HISA introduces a hierarchical indexing mechanism that improves indexer efficiency while keeping Sparse MLA identical to DSA. The notation introduced below is used throughout the rest of the paper.


Indexer in DSA.




Let LL denote the causal prefix length for a query position tt. The indexer maintains lightweight indexing keys 𝐤sI\mathbf{k}_{s}^{I}, indexing queries 𝐪t,jI\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{I} for HIH^{I} indexing heads, and per-head gating weights wt,jIw_{t,j}^{I}. The relevance score between query tt and key ss is




It,s=∑j=1HIwt,jI⋅ReLU⁡(𝐪t,jI⋅𝐤sI).I_{t,s}=\sum_{j=1}^{H^{I}}w_{t,j}^{I}\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{I}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{s}^{I}\right).

(1)


The indexer then selects the top-kk token indices,




𝒯t=TopK(It,:,k),\mathcal{T}_{t}=\mathrm{TopK}(I_{t,:},\,k),

(2)


which are passed to the downstream Sparse MLA operator. The per-query indexer cost is therefore 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L), dominated by the HIH^{I} head–token products in Eq. 1; aggregated over a full prefill it grows as 𝒪⁡(HI​L2)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L^{2}) per layer.



Sparse MLA in DSA.




Sparse MLA adopts the MQA mode of MLA, in which each token stores a single latent key–value entry 𝐜s\mathbf{c}_{s} shared across all query heads. Given the selected token set 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}, attention is computed only over the selected entries:




𝐮t=Attn⁡(𝐡t,{𝐜s∣s∈𝒯t}).\mathbf{u}_{t}=\mathrm{Attn}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_{t},\,\left\{\mathbf{c}_{s}\mid s\in\mathcal{T}_{t}\right\}\right).

(3)


This reduces the dominant attention cost from 𝒪⁡(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}) to 𝒪⁡(L​k)\mathcal{O}(Lk). The interface between the two components is exactly the selected token set 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}, which makes the indexer the natural target for further acceleration without touching Sparse MLA.



Indexer in HISA.




HISA replaces the flat prefix scan with a two-stage coarse-to-fine search. The prefix is partitioned into M=⌈L/B⌉M=\lceil L/B\rceil contiguous blocks ℬ1,…,ℬM\mathcal{B}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{B}_{M} of size BB, and each block is summarized by a representative key obtained via mean pooling:




𝐤~bI=Pool⁡({𝐤sI∣s∈ℬb}).\tilde{\mathbf{k}}_{b}^{I}=\mathrm{Pool}\!\left(\left\{\mathbf{k}_{s}^{I}\mid s\in\mathcal{B}_{b}\right\}\right).

(4)





In the first stage, the same indexing queries 𝐪t,jI\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{I} and gating weights wt,jIw_{t,j}^{I} as in DSA are reused to score the pooled keys, and the top-mm blocks are selected:




Jt,b=∑j=1HIwt,jI⋅ReLU(𝐪t,jI⋅𝐤~bI),𝒞t=TopK(Jt,:,m).J_{t,b}=\sum_{j=1}^{H^{I}}w_{t,j}^{I}\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{t,j}^{I}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{k}}_{b}^{I}\right),\quad\mathcal{C}_{t}=\mathrm{TopK}(J_{t,:},\,m).

(5)


Following [17], the first and last blocks are always included in 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} to retain the attention sink and local context. The candidate token set is then Ωt=⋃b∈𝒞tℬb\Omega_{t}=\bigcup_{b\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\mathcal{B}_{b}.




In the second stage, the original DSA scoring (Eq. 1) is applied within Ωt\Omega_{t}, and the final top-kk tokens




𝒯t=TopK⁡({It,s∣s∈Ωt},k)\mathcal{T}_{t}=\mathrm{TopK}\!\left(\left\{I_{t,s}\mid s\in\Omega_{t}\right\},\,k\right)

(6)


are passed to the unmodified Sparse MLA operator.





4 Method




As established in Section 3, the DSA indexer scores every prefix token with all HIH^{I} heads, giving a per-query cost of 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L) that already dominates the indexer kernel even after FP8 quantisation, the ReLU non-linearity, and the small indexer dimension used by DeepSeek-V3.2 [7]. The HIH^{I} heads cannot simply be collapsed into one: each specialises in a different relevance pattern, so reducing HIH^{I} measurably degrades retrieval. Our starting point is the observation that this expressiveness is needed only in aggregate—across all queries and across the prefix—whereas any single query is well served by a small, query-dependent subset of heads. The MISA method (Section 4.1) exploits this by routing such a subset on cheap block-level statistics; a hierarchical extension MISA† (Section 4.2) re-introduces the full head pool only on a small candidate set, recovering DSA’s exact selection.



4.1 MISA: mixture of indexer experts




We propose MISA (Mixture of Indexer Sparse Attention), shown alongside DSA in Figure 1. MISA treats the HIH^{I} indexer heads as a pool of experts and uses a lightweight router to select a small subset of h≪HIh\ll H^{I} active heads per query, in the spirit of MoE routing. The selected experts then perform the token-level scoring, while the routing decision itself is computed on cheap block-level statistics.

It is worth contrasting the role of block pooling here with that in HISA. In other words, block pooling is used here purely as a cheap proxy that avoids materializing the full 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L) tensor of head–token products when estimating which heads matter for the current query.

Why MoE in the indexer.




Standard MoE routes the FFN computation while keeping attention dense. MISA instead routes which similarity patterns are used to select tokens; the downstream attention itself remains dense over the chosen 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}. The key empirical observation that makes this practical is that the relevant indexer heads of a query change slowly across the prefix, so a coarse block-level estimate is sufficient to predict them, and the heavy token-level scan only needs to consult a small subset of heads.





4.2 Hierarchical MISA: coarse-to-fine indexing




The single-stage MISA above already cuts indexer cost substantially. We further extend it to a coarse-to-fine variant, denoted MISA†, in which a cheap MoE pass first prunes the prefix to a candidate set, and a second pass refines the candidates with the full DSA indexer. Crucially, the second stage of MISA† uses the DSA indexer (Eq. 1) on the candidate tokens; we do not adopt HISA’s block-level top-mm filtering at any stage.




In the coarse stage, the MoE scoring of Eq. 9 is used to select an enlarged candidate set

Comparison with HISA.




Both MISA† and HISA have a two-stage coarse-to-fine structure, but the granularity of the coarse pass is fundamentally different. HISA’s coarse pass operates at the block level: pooling discards intra-block variation and a block must be kept or discarded as a whole, so the candidate set Ωt\Omega_{t} is always a union of full blocks. MISA†, by contrast, keeps the coarse pass at full token granularity (Eq. 11) and reduces compute via head-level routing instead of block-level filtering, so tokens within the same block are still ranked individually. The fine pass is also stricter: it re-applies the original DSA scoring using all HIH^{I} heads on Ωt\Omega_{t}, whereas HISA’s fine pass operates on the union of selected blocks without revisiting the head set. Empirically, this combination yields a candidate set with consistently higher recall of DSA’s top-kk at the same compute budget (Appendix A), which in turn translates into the quality gains reported in Sections 5.1–5.2.






5 Experimental results




We evaluate MISA as a drop-in replacement for the indexer in DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), and verify that it preserves the retrieval and downstream quality of DSA / HISA at a fraction of the per-token compute. Unless stated otherwise, all sparse methods are applied at inference time without any additional training.


Models.




We use two open-weight long-context models that natively support DSA: DeepSeek-V3.2 [7] (HI=64H^{I}=64 indexer heads, H=128H=128 main-attention heads, single shared KV head) and GLM-5 [28] (HI=32H^{I}=32 indexer heads). All baselines (DSA, Block-Sparse, HISA) and all variants of MISA share the same Sparse Multi-Head Latent Attention operator and differ only in how the indexer produces the per-query token set 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}.



Default MISA hyperparameters.




The router uses a block size of B=1024B=1024, which is an order of magnitude larger than HISA’s B=128B=128 and yields a small number of pooled keys M=⌈L/B⌉M=\lceil L/B\rceil. The single-stage MISA routes hh active heads on the full prefix and selects k=2048k=2048 tokens directly. The hierarchical MISA† first uses the same MoE-routed scoring to retain k′=8192k^{\prime}=8192 candidates, then re-scores them with the full DSA indexer (all HIH^{I} heads) and keeps the top k=2048k=2048. Unless otherwise specified, we use h=8h=8 active heads in both prefill and decode, i.e. a 8×8\times reduction over DSA on DeepSeek-V3.2 and a 4×4\times reduction on GLM-5.



Baselines.




DSA is the original dense indexer of DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5, scoring every prefix token with all HIH^{I} indexer heads. Block-Sparse is a MoBA-style [17] inference-time selector: the prefix is partitioned into uniform blocks of size B=128B=128, each block is summarised by its mean indexing key, and the m=k/Bm=k/B blocks with the highest query-block inner product are retained as the selected token set (same overall token budget kk as all other methods). HISA [24] is the hierarchical indexer with block size B=128B=128, top-mm block filtering, and per-token refinement. The DSA, Block-Sparse, and HISA scores in Table 1 are taken from the HISA paper [24], while all other figures in this section are produced with our own implementation under matched hyperparameters.



Hardware and evaluation.




All experiments—LongBench evaluation, NIAH heatmaps, indexer-kernel benchmark, IoU computation, and the three ablation studies —are run on 8×\times NVIDIA H200 GPUs. We measure (i) downstream quality on LongBench, averaged across sub-tasks within each of six categories; (ii) Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval accuracy at context lengths up to 128K, sweeping needle depth from 0%0\% to 100%100\%; (iii) 1 and 2 stage MISA kernel latency of the indexer; and (iv) per-layer Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between the token set selected by a given method and the top-20482048 set selected by the full DSA indexer, which serves as the ground-truth reference for retrieval. Ablations on the router score Et,jE_{t,j}, the number of active heads hh, and the block size BB are all carried out on DeepSeek-V3.2. The IoU experiments and the majority of ablation experiments are provided in the appendix.

5.3 Indexer kernel speed




Figure 3 compares the wall-clock latency of the indexer kernel for DSA and MISA on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, under both the 1-stage (Fig. 3(a)) and 2-stage (Fig. 3(b),marked as MISA†) configurations. In contrast, MISA activates only h=8h=8 heads per query, scoring the prefix with complexity 𝒪⁡(L​h+M​HI)\mathcal{O}(Lh+MH^{I}), where the second term corresponds to the (negligible) router overhead applied on M=⌈L/B⌉≪LM=\lceil L/B\rceil\ll L pooled keys. In the 1-stage setting, the MISA kernel is consistently faster than DSA across the entire sequence-length range. In the 2-stage setting, it also outperforms DSA when the sequence length exceeds 32k. The asymptotic HI/h=8×H^{I}/h=8\times reduction in head–token products is not fully reflected in wall-clock latency—factors such as memory traffic, load imbalance introduced by the routed expert set, and a small but non-zero router overhead all reduce the theoretical speedup. Nevertheless, our TileLang implementation already achieves approximately a 3.82×3.82\times end-to-end speedup over DSA’s original indexer kernel for long contexts. This realized
speedup confirms that head-axis routing not only yields the quality benefits reported in Section 5, but also translates into measurable savings on real hardware.

6 Conclusion




We presented MISA, which serves as an MoE-style replacement for the DSA indexer. A lightweight block-pooled router selects a query-dependent subset of h≪HIh\ll H^{I} active heads, and only those heads run the heavy token-level scan. This single change cuts the dominant per-token cost of fine-grained sparse attention from 𝒪⁡(HI​L)\mathcal{O}(H^{I}L) to 𝒪⁡(h​L+HI​M)\mathcal{O}(hL+H^{I}M) while preserving the full diversity of the indexer pool, because every head remains available—routing simply chooses which ones to consult on each token. A coarse-to-fine extension, MISA†, additionally re-ranks an enlarged routed candidate set with the original DSA indexer and recovers the dense top-kk almost exactly.




Our experiments support the design on two open-weight long-context models. With h=8h=8 active heads (an 8×8\times head reduction on DeepSeek-V3.2 and a 4×4\times reduction on GLM-5) and no additional training, MISA matches the dense DSA indexer on LongBench within 0.50.5 average points, outperforms both Block-Sparse and HISA on average, and retains a fully green Needle-in-a-Haystack heatmap up to 128K context. Our TileLang kernel implementation translates these savings into roughly a 3.82×3.82\times wall-clock speedup over DSA’s original kernel on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU.




7 Limitation




Several questions regarding MISA remain unaddressed in this paper: (i) The speed experiments only measure the latency of the TileLang kernel rather than the end-to-end latency of the full model. (ii) Although the MoE-style indexer reduces the computational cost of the DSA stage, it does not reduce the memory access volume to the KV cache in that stage.(iii) All results in this paper are obtained by inserting MISA into pretrained DSA-based models without finetuning, jointly training the router with the indexer should further close the residual gap on the few categories where MISA trails the dense baseline. We will actively explore the aforementioned open questions. Nevertheless, the presented experiments have comprehensively validated the superiority of MISA. We hope our work will stimulate interest and encourage further exploration within the community.
